wrong: new int[n] with a negative n creates an empty array. | right: Creating an array with a negative length throws NegativeArraySizeException at run time.

[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: in maths, a[5] or a_5 names element 5, and 'new' means 'fresh, empty, ready to fill', so 'new int[5]' is read as 'element 5' or as an empty list that grows. Java rule: new int[n] allocates exactly n elements, indexed 0 to n-1, each already set to the default value, and the length can never change.
[1] misconception (M) -> ArraysGrow: wrong rule: An array grows as you add elements. Right rule: An array's length is fixed when it is created, so writing to a[n] throws an exception instead of adding a slot.
[2] misconception (M) -> ArrayAllocationWithoutNew: wrong rule: Arrays are created without the new keyword. Right rule: An array exists only after new T[n] (or an initializer list in a declaration, which implies creation) has run.
[3] misconception (M) -> ArrayLengthCannotBeZero: wrong rule: An array cannot have length 0. Right rule: new int[0] is a legal array with a.length == 0 (no element can be indexed).
[4] misconception (M) -> ArrayCreationIsFree: wrong rule: Creating a big array with new takes no time because the elements are not set yet. Right rule: Java initializes every element when the array is created, so creation takes time proportional to its length.
[5] inconsistent_trace (T) -> ArraysGrow: Points to LT: evaluate the size, allocate the array, fill it with defaults, return the reference, then assign it. Inconsistent application: the size n is treated as the last index on some lines, or the array is assumed to exist already at its declaration. (here mixing in: "an array grows as you add elements")
[6] misconception (M) -> ArrayRangeInclusive: wrong rule: new int[n] has slots 0 to n, inclusive. Right rule: new int[n] has exactly n slots, a[0] through a[n-1]; a[n] does not exist.
[7] misconception (M) -> DeclarationCreatesArray: wrong rule: int[] a; already makes an array that can be indexed. Right rule: Only new (or an initializer) creates the array; before that, using a[i] is the compile-time error 'variable a might not have been initialized'.
[8] misconception (M) -> ArrayBracketCountIsLength: wrong rule: The number of brackets in new int[][] is the array's length. Right rule: Bracket pairs give the number of dimensions; the length is the value of the dimension expression inside them.

[0] names_the_element (N): Identity: an array creation expression; new T[n] makes a new array object with n elements of type T and yields a reference to it.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Declarative: 'new T[expr]', where expr is any int-valued expression evaluated at run time; the resulting length is fixed for the array's lifetime.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Sequencing: (1) the dimension expression is evaluated; (2) if it is negative, NegativeArraySizeException is thrown; (3) space for n elements is reserved and every element is set to its default; (4) the expression yields the reference, which an enclosing assignment then stores.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Result: a value of type T[], namely a reference to a new array of length n whose elements all hold the default (0, 0.0, false or null). It produces no output; printing it shows an address, not the elements.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): State transition: one execution creates one new array object (n new element variables at their defaults) and returns its reference. No existing variable changes until that reference is assigned.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The declared element type must match the created one; in 'double[] a = new double[N];' the left side is the declaration and the right side is the creation.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Elements can be indexed only after creation, and the n given to new fixes the valid index range 0..n-1.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): Creation is what puts the default value (0, 0.0, false, null) in every slot; each execution of new gives fresh defaults.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): The size n given to new becomes a.length and never changes for that array object.
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): An initializer {v0, ..., vk} implies creation of an array of length k+1, so new is not written.
[5] relation_to_neighbour (R): Only new makes a distinct array. Assignment copies the reference, so a separate copy needs new plus an element-by-element copy.
[6] relation_to_neighbour (R): new yields the reference (address) of the array, and the array variable stores that reference, not the elements.
[7] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan/role: reserve storage for a number of values that may be known only at run time (e.g. N from the command line), before any value is stored.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> ArraysGrow: Conservation: changing n changes a.length and the valid index range but not the element type. Moving 'new' inside a loop gives a fresh array of defaults on every pass (SelfAvoidingWalk relies on this). Re-creating an array never changes arrays that other variables already refer to.
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The dimension expression of new must be >= 0. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: the size evaluates to a negative int, e.g. a negative command-line value, or int overflow such as new int[N*N*N*N] with N = 1000 (NegativeArraySizeException)
[2] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Applicability: use new T[n] when the number of values is known (at least at run time) before they are stored and stays fixed. Use an initializer when the values are compile-time constants, and a resizing structure when the count is unknown in advance.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: An array must be allocated with new before its elements are accessed. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: 'int[] a;' followed by a[i] = ... with no creation (variable a might not have been initialized)
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The dimension expression must have an integral type (int after promotion). Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: a double or long size such as new int[2.5] or new int[n] with long n (incompatible types: possible lossy conversion)
[5] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The requested array must fit in the memory available to Java. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: a very large n such as new boolean[N+1] for huge N in PrimeSieve (OutOfMemoryError)

Because new creates one array and the variable stores only a reference to it, assigning that variable to another makes both names refer to the same array.
new fills every slot with the type's default value: 0, 0.0, false or null.
{v0, v1, ..., vk} is a shorthand that creates an array of length k + 1 and fills it in one step.
When an array is created, the array name stores the memory address of its values; a[i] is found by adding i to that address.
An array must be created with new before any of its elements a[i] can be accessed.
The size n given to new becomes a.length and stays fixed for the array's lifetime.
Sampling without replacement first creates an array of all candidates (perm), then picks from the part not yet chosen.
double[] a; declares the array name and type; a = new double[N]; then creates the array.
